systems_owned.name: MySQL to Postgres, live
systems_owned.summary: Two-way bridge between a fifteen-year-old MySQL estate and new Postgres services, with no maintenance window. A one-time historical backfill (read-only snapshot, stated cut-off, re-runnable) kept strictly separate from a continuous reverse sync into legacy tables; idempotency guards in the data; drift detection; a mapping spec precise enough that someone else could run the cutover. Migrated by domain, not by table, so each phase was independently reversible. Lesson: instrument reconciliation from day one.

migration_case_study.title: Moving a live commerce platform between two databases without a maintenance window
migration_case_study.context: B2B commerce platform selling annual seat-based contracts; six product lines, each with its own pricing shape; a dozen services; a ~15-year-old MySQL estate replaced by domain services on PostgreSQL, both live with customers throughout. Legacy products were not retired, so the result was two systems of record, both live, converging slowly.
options_rejected: Freeze, dump, restore: unbounded failure mode, no quick way back from a failed restore
Big-bang cutover behind a flag: concentrates all risk in one moment; partial cutovers have no real recovery
Strangler at the edge only: legacy products still read shared identity and subscription records the same day
Application-layer dual-write alone: not one transaction across two engines; correctness that depends on discipline is not correctness
design: Two flows kept strictly separate, with separate code, schedules and failure modes
Flow one: one-time historical backfill, legacy to new, from a read-only snapshot, bounded by a stated historical cut-off, designed to be re-runnable
Flow two: continuous reverse sync, new to legacy, so legacy products keep reading; the new system is the system of record and legacy is a projection of it

Schema: ~30 product-partitioned legacy tables became four generic ones (order, line item, item detail, configuration); product identity moved from table names into columns and a JSON configuration with its own derivation spec
Ordering enforced by the runner: organisations before orders, orders before users and subscriptions
Idempotency in the data, not the runbook: an order is ported only when its external-origin identifier is null, so CRM-originated records are never duplicated

numbers.timeline: Under six months from first specification to steady state
numbers.records_backfilled: 500k+, consolidated from two upstream systems of record
numbers.specification: ~25,000 words across seven documents; designed and specified by me, executed by a platform team

migration_case_study.lesson: In any dual-write system drift is not a risk, it is a certainty with an unknown arrival time. Reconciliation must exist before the first write; it is part of the mechanism, not a phase after it.
would_do_differently: Write the configuration derivation before the transfer mechanism
Decide and state the historical cut-off on page one
Separate the two flows explicitly, sooner
principles: Separate the one-time historical port from continuous sync
Treat reconciliation as part of the mechanism

projects.name: claude-toolkit
projects.summary: Ten small, dependency-free CLI tools (Python 3) that make AI-assisted coding sessions safer and cheaper: MCP server toggling with restorable config, a macOS Keychain vault so an agent can use a credential without seeing it, DB access that keeps passwords out of shell history, output compression, offline code/schema/session indexes, a zero-token daily work log, and an offline Jira/Confluence fetcher.
tools: claude-toggle: enable/disable MCP servers without losing config; profiles, backups, restore
claude-vault: secrets in the macOS Keychain, used by AI sessions without being seen
db-conn: Postgres and MySQL queries using vault-stored credentials; production read-only unless --write
squeeze: compresses verbose command output before it enters the transcript
cindex: per-project code index for compact path:line search results
dbindex: offline schema index for all vault database connections
csession: indexes Claude Code sessions by task, with resume-vs-new suggestions and briefs
toolkit: installs every tool and verifies the setup (install, doctor)
worklog: zero-token daily work logs from csession and git data
atl: offline Jira and Confluence fetcher that outputs compact TSV or text
design_principles: Secrets used, not seen; never pass a secret as a CLI argument
Reversible changes: stash instead of delete, back up before every change
Safe defaults: dry-run and read-only unless explicitly overridden
Token efficiency: compact output and cheap offline lookups over live queries

working_principles: Specification before implementation: write the spec first, then review the code against it
Schema before endpoint: the schema is what you end up living with
Reversible steps over big-bang cutovers: every migration run could be rolled back at any point
Code review is where the real engineering standard gets set, more than in a style guide
leadership_philosophy: Write the specification, then review against it — make the disagreement happen before the code exists, when it is cheap.
Code review is where teaching happens — the main quality surface and the main development surface at once; built an AI reviewer to take the mechanical half off people's plates.
Guiding ten is different from managing one — influence at that width comes from the artefacts you leave behind: specs, schemas, review comments, service boundaries.
